summary: God appoints Bezalel, Oholiab, and other skilled workers to make the sanctuary, furnishings, garments, oil, and incense according to the instructions. The Sabbath is reaffirmed as a covenant sign with severe penalties for violation, and the mountain speech ends with Moses receiving the two stone tablets written with God's finger.
whyItMatters: The work receives named makers and divine enablement, yet sacred construction remains framed by a command to rest. The delivery of the tablets closes the instructions just before the narrative reveals a breach of covenant below the mountain.

context.author: Exodus does not name its final author. It records Moses writing particular covenant material; traditional Mosaic attribution and modern accounts of composition are distinguished in the book briefing.
context.audience: Israel remembering its rescue from Egypt and its obligations as a covenant community. The chapter does not identify an individual dedicatee.
context.date: The narrative places these events at Sinai after the departure from Egypt. The date of the events and the history of the book’s composition are separate, debated questions.
context.setting: The conclusion of God's sanctuary instructions to Moses on Mount Sinai.
context.literaryForm: Craftsmen's commissioning, a Sabbath covenant speech, and a brief narrative notice about the tablets.

before.text: The preceding chapter has completed further sanctuary requirements, including restricted oil and incense. The people who will carry out this detailed work are now identified.

here.text: Craft and covenant are joined: wisdom equips the workers, Sabbath marks the community, and the written tablets complete the mountain encounter.

after.text: While Moses is delayed, the people ask Aaron for gods to lead them, and the making of a gold calf begins the covenant crisis.

outline.heading: Bezalel’s calling and capacities
outline.note: God names and equips him for metal, stone, and woodwork.

outline.heading: Coworkers and the assigned work
outline.note: Oholiab and other skilled people join in making the full range of sanctuary items.

outline.heading: Sabbath as sign, rest, and covenant
outline.note: Its holiness and creation pattern accompany explicit death and exclusion sanctions.

outline.heading: The tablets given
outline.note: Moses receives the stone covenant tablets at the end of the divine speech.

keyVerses.text: I have filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship,
keyVerses.why: Divine empowerment is described through concrete wisdom, knowledge, and workmanship.

keyVerses.text: “Speak also to the children of Israel, saying, ‘Most certainly you shall keep my Sabbaths; for it is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, that you may know that I am Yahweh who sanctifies you.
keyVerses.why: Sabbath is identified as a sign that God sanctifies the people.

keyVerses.text: When he finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, he gave Moses the two tablets of the covenant, stone tablets, written with God’s finger.
keyVerses.why: The written tablets close the instructions and become a central object in the coming crisis.

questions.question: What is Bezalel equipped to do?
questions.answer: The Spirit of God fills him with wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and workmanship for metals, stone setting, and wood carving. The specific tasks make the gift concrete in materials and skilled labor.

questions.question: Does Bezalel work alone?
questions.answer: Oholiab is appointed with him, and wisdom is also given to other wise-hearted workers. The chapter names leaders while describing a broader body of people able to carry out the assigned work.

questions.question: What does “wise-hearted” mean in the work assignment?
questions.answer: It identifies people endowed with the wisdom to make what God has commanded. Here that wisdom is expressed in practical competence for the listed crafts.

questions.question: How broad is their commission?
questions.answer: It includes the tent and furnishings, both altars, the basin, priestly garments, anointing oil, and incense. The list gathers the preceding specifications into a shared task whose standard is what has been commanded.

questions.question: Why is Sabbath placed after instructions for so much work?
questions.answer: The next speech insists that Israel must keep the Sabbaths as a sign of God's sanctifying relationship. Its placement puts the skilled labor beside an obligation to stop, while the creation pattern supplies the stated six-days-and-one rhythm.

questions.question: What penalties accompany the Sabbath command?
questions.answer: The text expressly orders death for profaning the Sabbath or working on it and also speaks of being cut off. The sign of covenant identity is enforced here through lethal sanctions within the ancient community.

questions.question: Does “God’s finger” provide a full account of how the tablets were produced?
questions.answer: The narrator attributes the stone tablets' writing to God using that bodily image. It emphasizes divine authorship of the covenant tablets without describing a process a reader could reconstruct or a complete physical account of God.

glossary.def: The practical capacity for metalwork, stone cutting, wood carving, and other assigned crafts.
The seventh-day rest identified here as a continuing covenant sign between God and Israel.
The two stone surfaces on which the covenant is written and which Moses receives.
